sections.title: Background
sections.tldr: Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed when blood pressure drops by ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. This condition reflects sympathetic nervous system dysfunction and can be classified as neurogenic when compensatory heart rate increases are absent or minimal. (10 sources)
sections.text:
Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a systolic blood pressure fall of ≥20 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure fall of ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or active postural change from supine to upright position <Paper corpusId="10288622" paperTitle="(Garruti et al., 2012)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="203568317" paperTitle="(Bilici et al., 2019)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="221672374" paperTitle="(Oh, 2020)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="257099301" paperTitle="(Brignole et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="271033434" paperTitle="(Huang et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="3551360" paperTitle="(Tsiompanidis et al., 2018)" isShortName></Paper>. Some definitions also include a standing systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg as diagnostic criteria <Paper corpusId="257099301" paperTitle="(Brignole et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

The condition reflects sympathetic nervous system dysfunction and can be further classified based on timing and underlying pathophysiology <Paper corpusId="10288622" paperTitle="(Garruti et al., 2012)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="25766017" paperTitle="(Low et al., 1975)" isShortName></Paper>. Classic orthostatic hypotension occurs within 3 minutes of standing, while delayed orthostatic hypotension manifests after more than 3 minutes <Paper corpusId="278707790" paperTitle="(Klemm et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>.

A key diagnostic distinction is made between neurogenic and non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension based on the heart rate response. In neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, compensatory tachycardia does not appear or is minimal because parasympathetic fiber loss begins earlier than sympathetic denervation <Paper corpusId="221672374" paperTitle="(Oh, 2020)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="211031022" paperTitle="(Mobarek, 2020)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="5321136" paperTitle="(Freeman, 2008)" isShortName></Paper>. This lack of adequate compensatory heart rate increase upon standing is consistent with a neurogenic cause and represents an important clinical finding for diagnosis and management <Paper corpusId="211031022" paperTitle="(Mobarek, 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

snippets: Tests of autonomic function were performed on 16 subjects with diabetic neuropathy. Abnormal sweating occurred in 10/10 (100 per cent), postural hypotension in 7/16 (44 per cent), an abnormal Valsalva ratio in 7/11 (64 per cent), and denervation hypersensitivity to phenylephrine in 2/8 (25 per cent) of patients tested. A quantitative assessment of baroreceptor function was made. In diabetics, there was a reduced resting heart period, heart period range and mean gain. Quantitative histological studies were performed on the greater splanchnic nerves removed at autopsy from 9 control subjects and from 8 subjects with diabetic neuropathy. The fibre density was significantly reduced in the greater splanchnic nerve of diabetics. The predominant pathology on teased fibre preparations was that of demyelination. Disordered blood pressure control in diabetes correlated with the pathological abnormalities in the sympathetic nervous system. Light and electronmicroscopic studies were performed on the sural nerves of 2 diabetic subjects with autonomic dysfunction. The predominant change was active axonal degeneration affecting mainly unmyelinated and small myelinated fibres.

sections.title: Heart Rate Response Parameters
sections.tldr: The key ECG parameter for diagnosing neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is the ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio, where a value <0.5 bpm/mmHg indicates neurogenic causes. Additionally, a blunted heart rate increase of <17 bpm upon standing helps distinguish neurogenic from non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. (9 sources)
sections.text:
The most important ECG-derived parameter for diagnosing neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is the ratio of heart rate change to systolic blood pressure change (ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio). A ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio <0.5 bpm/mmHg within 3 minutes of standing indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and provides a sensitive and specific cutoff value <Paper corpusId="232273554" paperTitle="(Thijs et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="238901314" paperTitle="(Naschitz, 2020)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="248296443" paperTitle="(Wenning et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>. This ratio reflects cardiac baroreflex gain and is considered more physiologically relevant than analyzing heart rate changes alone <Paper corpusId="253522551" paperTitle="(Lamotte et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

Studies have shown that the optimal threshold of <0.492 bpm/mmHg demonstrates excellent diagnostic performance, with sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 88% for detecting neurogenic orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="53009129" paperTitle="(Balagny et al., 2018)" isShortName></Paper>. External validation in patients with pure autonomic failure confirmed the excellent sensitivity of this ratio at 93% <Paper corpusId="54167902" paperTitle="(Waubant, 2018)" isShortName></Paper>.

In addition to the ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio, the absolute heart rate increase upon standing serves as a complementary diagnostic parameter. A heart rate increase of <17 bpm has optimal sensitivity (79%) and specificity (87%) for identifying neurogenic orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="53009129" paperTitle="(Balagny et al., 2018)" isShortName></Paper>. Some guidelines suggest that in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, the heart rate increase is usually ≤20 bpm, while marked increases suggest non-neurogenic causes <Paper corpusId="5926147" paperTitle="(Kaufmann et al., 2017)" isShortName></Paper>.

It is important to note that medications affecting heart rate response, such as beta blockers, should be excluded when interpreting these parameters <Paper corpusId="248296443" paperTitle="(Wenning et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>. The lack of adequate compensatory heart rate increase upon standing, as demonstrated by these parameters, provides crucial diagnostic information for distinguishing neurogenic from non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="211031022" paperTitle="(Mobarek, 2020)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="5321136" paperTitle="(Freeman, 2008)" isShortName></Paper>.

snippets: A simple bedside test to distinguish neurogenic from non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension (OH) is the ratio of heart rate increase to the simultaneous decrease in systolic blood pressure during OH (ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio) [1]. Since the heart rate response to hypotension is pronounced in patients with non-neurogenic OH but is blunted in those with efferent baroreflex failure, a ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio < 0.5 indicates baroreflex failure and is considered to provide a sensitive and specific cutoff value during active standing (Norcliffe-Kaufmann et al., 2018).

sections.title: ECG-derived Heart Rate Variability Parameters
sections.tldr: Heart rate variability (HRV) parameters from ECG can help assess autonomic function in orthostatic hypotension, though they are primarily research tools rather than clinical diagnostic measures. Key parameters include expiration-inspiration ratios, Valsalva ratios, and various HRV metrics that correlate with syncope severity and autonomic dysfunction. (6 sources)
sections.text:
While heart rate variability has been used to detect autonomic nervous system dysfunction, it remains primarily a research tool and is not useful for clinical diagnosis of autonomic dysfunction <Paper corpusId="195871860" paperTitle="(Allan, 2019)" isShortName></Paper>. However, several ECG-derived HRV parameters show promise for understanding the severity and characteristics of orthostatic hypotension.

Traditional autonomic function tests using ECG measurements include heart rate responses to deep breathing, with expiration-inspiration (E:I) ratios serving as key parameters <Paper corpusId="271033434" paperTitle="(Huang et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="22220536" paperTitle="(Balcioglu et al., 2015)" isShortName></Paper>. Studies have shown that differences between expiration and inspiration (E-I differences), E:I ratios, and Valsalva ratios were smaller in patients with orthostatic hypotension compared to those without <Paper corpusId="220499759" paperTitle="(Kim et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. In multivariate analysis, decreased Valsalva ratio was found to be an independent predictor of orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="220499759" paperTitle="(Kim et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

The measurement of expiration/inspiration heart rate variability is typically assessed using 3-lead ECG traces during paced deep breathing at six breaths per minute in a supine position, with maximum and minimum heart rates measured during each breathing cycle <Paper corpusId="221937213" paperTitle="(Hansen et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. Additionally, the 30:15 ratio, representing heart rate response to standing, serves as another parameter for assessing parasympathetic function <Paper corpusId="271033434" paperTitle="(Huang et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="22220536" paperTitle="(Balcioglu et al., 2015)" isShortName></Paper>.

Advanced HRV analysis using 24-hour Holter monitoring has revealed correlations between various HRV parameters and syncope characteristics in orthostatic hypotension patients. Notable correlations include the relationship between syncope frequency and SDANN (r=-0.62) and RMSSD (r=-0.46), as well as correlations between syncope duration and LF/HF ratio (r=0.57) <Paper corpusId="268490035" paperTitle="(Kovalchuk, 2022)" isShortName></Paper>. These findings suggest that HRV parameters may help assess the severity of autonomic dysfunction in orthostatic hypotension, though their clinical utility remains limited to research applications.

snippets: Cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN) is a frequent chronic complication of diabetes mellitus with potentially life-threatening outcomes. CAN is caused by the impairment of the autonomic nerve fibers regulating heart rate, cardiac output, myocardial contractility, cardiac electrophysiology and blood vessel constriction and dilatation. It causes a wide range of cardiac disorders, including resting tachycardia, arrhythmias, intraoperative cardiovascular instability, asymptomatic myocardial ischemia and infarction and increased rate of mortality after myocardial infarction. Etiological factors associated with autonomic neuropathy include insufficient glycemic control, a longer period since the onset of diabetes, increased age, female sex and greater body mass index. The most commonly used methods for the diagnosis of CAN are based upon the assessment of heart rate variability (the physiological variation in the time interval between heartbeats), as it is one of the first findings in both clinically asymptomatic and symptomatic patients. Clinical symptoms associated with CAN generally occur late in the disease process and include early fatigue and exhaustion during exercise, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, presyncope and syncope. Treatment is based on early diagnosis, life style changes, optimization of glycemic control and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Medical therapies, including aldose reductase inhibitors, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, prostoglandin analogs and alpha-lipoic acid, have been found to be effective in randomized controlled trials. The following article includes the epidemiology, clinical findings and cardiovascular consequences, diagnosis, and approaches to prevention and treatment of CAN.

sections.title: QTc Interval and Other ECG Parameters
sections.tldr: QTc interval prolongation is a key ECG finding in orthostatic hypotension, with longer QTc intervals correlating with worse autonomic dysfunction. Additional ECG abnormalities including rhythm disturbances, conduction blocks, and ST deviations can help identify high-risk patients with syncope. (3 sources)
sections.text:
The QTc interval represents one of the most important ECG parameters in orthostatic hypotension, serving as a biomarker for autonomic dysfunction. Patients with orthostatic hypotension show significantly prolonged QTc intervals (448.8±33.6 msec) compared to controls, along with increased QTc dispersion (59.5±30.3 msec) <Paper corpusId="52801845" paperTitle="(Kim et al., 2014)" isShortName></Paper>. This QTc prolongation correlates negatively with measures of autonomic function, including heart rate response to deep breathing (r = −0.443, p<0.001) and Valsalva ratio (r = −0.425, p<0.001) <Paper corpusId="52801845" paperTitle="(Kim et al., 2014)" isShortName></Paper>.

The prolonged QTc interval may be considered a biomarker for detecting alterations in sympathovagal balance, particularly cardiovagal dysfunction in orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="52801845" paperTitle="(Kim et al., 2014)" isShortName></Paper>. Additional correlations have been found between 24-hour average QT duration and various heart rate variability parameters, including SDANN (r=0.64, p=0.001) and RMSSD (r=0.63, p=0.002) in patients with syncope due to orthostatic hypotension <Paper corpusId="268490035" paperTitle="(Kovalchuk, 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

Beyond QTc intervals, other ECG abnormalities serve as important risk stratification tools. In patients with syncope, several ECG parameters predict high-risk presentations, including the presence of tachycardia, abnormal rhythms, wide QRS complexes, abnormal ST deviations, abnormal cardiac axis, and atrioventricular blocks <Paper corpusId="12524557" paperTitle="(Kayayurt et al., 2012)" isShortName></Paper>. The presence of any abnormal ECG findings combined represents a significant predictor of high-risk syncope in univariate analysis <Paper corpusId="12524557" paperTitle="(Kayayurt et al., 2012)" isShortName></Paper>.

The PQ interval also shows clinical relevance, with correlations found between 24-hour average PQ duration and heart rate variability parameters such as SDANN (r=0.64, p=0.001) and RMSSD (r=0.63, p=0.002) in orthostatic hypotension patients with syncope <Paper corpusId="268490035" paperTitle="(Kovalchuk, 2022)" isShortName></Paper>. These findings suggest that comprehensive ECG assessment beyond simple heart rate measurements provides valuable diagnostic and prognostic information in orthostatic hypotension.

sections.title: General ECG Assessment in Orthostatic Hypotension
sections.tldr: ECG monitoring is mandatory in all cases of syncope and orthostatic hypotension evaluation. Continuous ECG recording during orthostatic testing provides essential monitoring of heart rate changes and helps detect arrhythmias, while 12-lead ECG assessment identifies clinically significant abnormalities. (5 sources)
sections.text:
Electrocardiographic assessment forms a core component of orthostatic hypotension evaluation, with ECG being mandatory in all cases of syncope <Paper corpusId="239528751" paperTitle="(Nemani, 2018)" isShortName></Paper>. The timing of ECG acquisition is particularly important, with immediate ECG recommended when suspicion of arrhythmia is strong <Paper corpusId="239528751" paperTitle="(Nemani, 2018)" isShortName></Paper>.

During orthostatic testing, continuous ECG monitoring serves multiple purposes beyond simple heart rate measurement. Beat-to-beat ECG monitoring allows for precise calculation of heart rate changes, with studies using 30-second averaging periods to determine mean heart rate values in supine position, after 3 minutes of head-up tilt, and at the point of lowest blood pressure during passive orthostasis <Paper corpusId="6589381" paperTitle="(Nilsson et al., 2015)" isShortName></Paper>. This continuous monitoring approach enables detection of both immediate and time-dependent neuronal and hormonal effects of orthostatic stress <Paper corpusId="224822399" paperTitle="(Wang et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

The ECG assessment protocol typically involves recording during standardized conditions, with patients lying supine for at least 10 minutes before testing, followed by continuous monitoring during the orthostatic challenge <Paper corpusId="17098936" paperTitle="(Tan et al., 2006)" isShortName></Paper>. Advanced monitoring systems can provide simultaneous ECG and blood pressure recording, allowing for comprehensive cardiovascular assessment during postural changes <Paper corpusId="224822399" paperTitle="(Wang et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

Clinical interpretation of ECG findings requires systematic evaluation for abnormalities and assessment of clinical significance. Healthcare providers routinely review ECGs alongside chest radiographs to identify any abnormalities and determine their clinical relevance in the context of orthostatic symptoms <Paper corpusId="247308214" paperTitle="(Kenny et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>. This comprehensive approach ensures that ECG findings are properly integrated into the overall diagnostic assessment of orthostatic hypotension and related cardiovascular conditions.

snippets: Continuous blood pressure and ECG were recorded from individuals with SCI (n = 159) and non‐injured individuals (n = 48)

Digitized blood pressure and heart rate signals were analyzed with a custom program (MATLAB, the MathWorks, Natick, MA) that performed R-peak detection of ECG, and peak and trough detection of the blood pressure waveform. Continuous heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure are summarized as the mean of 5-min in the supine position to estimate resting blood pressure and heart rate, and 1-min means during the seated position to account for time-dependent neuronal and hormonal effects to orthostatic stress (Rowell, 1993); change was calculated as the difference between each one-minute seated mean from the supine mean. Criteria for the incidence of orthostatic hypotension was defined as a decrease in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min upon the assumption of an upright position, based on the definition established by the American Academy of Neurology and the American Autonomic Society (AAS/AAN, 1996). Orthostatic hypotension was determined from the difference between the lowest mean systolic and/or diastolic blood pressure that occurred within the first 3 min of an upright position and the 5-min supine mean.

A drop in blood pressure of ≥20 mm Hg systolic or ≥10 mm Hg diastolic was considered consistent with orthostatic hypotension. A sustained increase in heart rate of >30 beats per minute above supine heart rate, without a drop in blood pressure, was considered consistent with postural tachycardia.

Electrocardiographs (ECGs) and chest radiographs (CXRs) were reviewed by a clinician who evaluated the presence of abnormalities and judged if any changes present were clinically significant.
